news_communities.title: State Primary Election 2026: Democratic challengers outspend state Rep. Wong in their quest for his Ninth Essex House District seat
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
By Mark E. Vogler

 

The two Democratic candidates from Lynn who face each other in the Sept. 1 State Primary have both spent more on their respective campaigns to dethrone longtime state Rep. Donald Wong (R-Saugus) in the race for the Ninth Essex House District seat than the incumbent. Peter Meaney has already spent $157,512.34 and has $110,840.22 in cash on hand, according to documents filed through July 31 with the state Office of Campaign and Political Finance (OCPF). Meaney is a Lynn dentist who was elected to a second term representing Ward 1 on the Lynn City Council last fall.

Meanwhile, Zosia VanMeter has spent $14,926.84 and has $15,311.23 in cash on hand, according to the OCPF. VanMeter has worked the last four and a half years in Lynn city government – including the last three years as acting and later permanent director of the Inspectional Division.

Rep. Wong, 74, who has no Republican competition in the primary, has spent $11,726.71 so far this year and has $22,820.21 left to spend on his campaign.

Collectively, the three candidates have spent more than $184,000 and have close to $149,000 in cash on hand, according to the OCPF.

He has been a community leader in Saugus for more than two decades. And since his election to the Legislature in 2010, he’s been a local leader for three communities. Wong, who has faced no opposition during the last three (2020, 2022 and 2024) elections, seeks his 9th two-year term representing the voters of the Ninth Essex House District. Precincts 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 in Saugus make up the core of the district, which also includes parts of Lynn and Wakefield.

Before getting elected to the State House, Wong served as chairman of the Saugus Board of Selectmen (2007-2011) and was a member of the Saugus Annual Town Meeting (2005-2007). He is a third-generation Chinese American. He, along with state Rep. Tackey Chan (D-Quincy), were the first Asian Americans elected to the state Legislature in 2010.

Wong and his wife Jeannie have three grown children. He is a businessman and president of Kowloon Group, Inc. which manages the Kowloon Restaurant – a popular Route 1 restaurant owned by three generations of his family at the same location for more than 75 years.

news_communities.title: Vandals destroy picnic tables at World Series Park
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Police are investigating reports of “massive vandalism” over the weekend (August 14-15) at World Series Park at 25 Dow St., behind Belmonte STEAM Academy. Bob Davis, the superintendent of the park, reported the destruction of the picnic benches under the pavilion and observed that one bench was placed on the pitcher’s mound.

“This vandalism doesn’t make sense,” Davis said this week.

“What kind of enjoyment does anyone get from destroying the property of others? Those benches and the pavilion are for the enjoyment of people attending baseball games. We will be looking at surveillance video to try to identify those responsible. As a result of this kind of destruction, we’re thinking of eliminating the picnic benches,” he said.

Davis reported seeing two individuals under the pavilion at about 11:30 p.m. on Saturday.

Anyone with information about the vandalism is asked to contact Saugus Police at 781-941-1125.

Vandalism at the park has been a problem in recent years despite the existence of surveillance cameras.

news_communities.title: Back to School
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Veteran Lynn Public School teacher Amanda O’Brien embraces a new career challenge as Assistant Principal at Belmonte STEAM Academy

 

By Mark E. Vogler

 

Hiring a second assistant principal to help administer Belmonte STEAM Academy was a top priority for school Principal Christopher Blair this summer as he prepared for his second year overseeing the upper elementary school that educates students in grades 2 through 5. “I really wanted to find somebody as capable as Heidi [Jimenez],” he said, referring to his vice principal from last year,” in an interview this week with The Saugus Advocate.

“Heidi was grown in the lab to be an assistant principal, and I was looking for another one just like her. Belmonte is a very big school and it’s very difficult to run without two capable assistant principals. If I have two capable assistant principals, the place runs like a dream. I’m happy to say I have that now,” he said.

From a job search that included 15 candidates, Blair said, he decided to hire Amanda O’Brien, a Lynn native who spent the past 11 years as a teacher in that city’s public school system. She was one of about 20 new staff members – and one of two assistant principals – who were hired by Saugus Public Schools for the 2026-27 academic year that begins Sept. 2. O’Brien, a 2010 graduate from St. Mary’s High School in Lynn, spent the past 11 years as a teacher employed by Lynn Public Schools.

“Amanda is very capable and she’s learning very quickly,” Blair said of the number three person in charge at the school. The principal said he was impressed with her “the second she sat down” for the job interview.

“She had read our student handbook. One of the things I had put in last year was the disciplinary plan. She had read it and spoke intelligently about the disciplinary plan,” Blair said.

“She had the presence of mind to read that handbook in advance of the interview. I was impressed, and she’s been that good since we hired her,” he said.

O’Brien’s primary role will be as the new Assistant Principal for Grades 2 and 4 at the Belmonte STEAM Academy.

Hiring O’Brien was crucial to being able to maintain a safe and well-run school, according to Blair. “My number one responsibility as an administrator is safety. We have a total of 850 kids coming into the building every day, and 850 have to go home,” he said.

“Once I know that number [number of students enrolled], if I have two great assistant principals, I know the school is that much safer. You’re going to have better teachers, better supervision and better visibility for us,” Blair said.

“And if you are better organized, you are going to have more ways to help students who are having a bad day,” he said.

O’Brien is a passionate educator, who walks around with a big smile, exuding great love for her profession. “I knew I wanted to be a teacher as early as I can remember,” said O’Brien, who lives in Salem with her husband Sean and their two children – Emersyn, who is six, and Jamie, who is four.

“You could always find me playing ‘school’ with my cousins and sister. I was drawn to helping young kids and seeing that lightbulb go off when something they’ve been struggling with finally clicked,” she said. “As I worked, I’ve continued to reflect, learn and grow as an educator by adding several teaching licenses throughout my tenure as a teacher. I am always looking for opportunities to strengthen my practice, build my skills and continue finding new ways to help students and teachers thrive.”

O’Brien received her Bachelor’s of Science in Elementary Education, with a concentration in Teaching Mathematics, at Wheelock College in 2014. A year later, she earned her Master’s of Science in International Teaching and Global Learning, with a concentration in English Learners, from Wheelock College. The college closed in 2018 and is now part of Boston University. In addition, O’Brien obtained a Certificate of Advanced Graduate Studies (CAGS) in Educational Leadership at Salem State University in 2026.

“When I am not at school, you will find me reading (or listening to) books, and spending time with my husband, Sean, and our children, or with friends,” O’Brien said. “We love eating ice cream and playing outside!”

O’Brien said she is thrilled to embark on a new phase of her educational career with Saugus Public Schools, in a place where she loves the small town “community feel.” “Everybody knows somebody in Saugus,” she said.

“I’ve spent the last 11 years working a variety of roles in the Lynn Public Schools. I started my career as a third grade teacher, moved up to fifth grade for several years. I have also been a math teacher and an English Language Learner teacher for students in grades 2-5. Most recently, I was a curriculum instruction teacher, working with both small groups of students and assisting teachers for the last two years,” O’Brien said.

“I love challenging myself, which has led me here to Saugus. During my master’s program I lived in Athens, Greece, with my best friend to teach at the American International School while completing my Master’s of Science in International Teaching and Global Learning, where I graduated from Wheelock College in 2015,” she said.

O’Brien has high expectations for her new career challenge as well as the future of Saugus Public Schools. “I stand by four core principles: collaboration, maintaining high expectations, equity and joy,” O’Brien said. “I firmly believe that all students can learn and grow with the appropriate supports and resources. Schools cannot succeed without people actively working together. I cannot wait to see all we’ll accomplish together.”

news_communities.title: Saugus Olympics Day is five weeks away
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
Boys & Girls Club and Challenger Baseball will benefit

 

Saugus Olympics Day at World Series Park in Saugus will be held on Sept. 26 from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. For nine years World Series Park has hosted a Special Olympics Day, raising $150,000 for Special Olympics. The event has been revived this year as a fundraiser that will benefit Challenger Baseball and the Boys & Girls Club.

“This type of event has great meaning and satisfaction, so we wanted to bring it back this year with different non-profit organizations,” Superintendent of World Series Park Bob Davis said in a recent statement.

A baseball tournament involving Challenger Baseball teams from the area will start at 9 a.m. At 11 a.m., the opening ceremony and parade of athletes will take place. Several dignitaries will take part. Gerry Agganis will throw out the first pitch.

Nancy Kerrigan, a former Olympics medalist in figure skating, will be available to meet & greet those in attendance. Other former Olympics medalists have also been invited to participate. The Olympic athletes will be honored during the opening ceremony.

Entertainment will start on the stage at 10 a.m. and will be provided by the Saugus High Chorus, the Memorylaners featuring Howie “Sachmo” Conley, Beat ConnXtionz dancers, Just The Tree of Us, the Rosa Singers and Joey B-Bop. The whole day will take on a festival atmosphere: raffles, a moon bounce, antique cars, booths, carnival games, hayrides, costumed characters and a large variety of food and drinks. Admission to the event is free and the public is invited and encouraged to attend. The rain date will be the next day, Sunday, September 27.

World Series Park is proud to again sponsor this type of event, with all proceeds going to Challenger Baseball and the Boys & Girls Club. Donations from businesses and individuals can be made prior to that day and will be acknowledged at the event. A fishbowl will be available for donations at the event. All checks should be made payable to World Series Park, 8 Holden Ave., Saugus, MA 01906.

news_communities.title: The Sounds of Saugus
news_communities.author: Jim Mitchell
news_communities.summary:
By Mark E. Vogler

 

Good morning, Saugus

September is such a busy month, I think I will need a secretary to keep track of all of those important dates that town residents might want to know about. Better yet, I will give our readers 10 days’ notice on the important ones I know about.

  • For starters, Tuesday, Sept. 1, is the day of the State Primary Election – which was the subject of our cover story last week. In next Friday’s newspaper, we’ll provide a preview of the important races and where people can vote in the town’s 10 precincts.
  • It’s BACK TO SCHOOL time again for Saugus Public Schools, like most public school districts across the state. Except, Labor Day is a little later this year, while school will begin in September. The first day of classes for students in grades 6 through 12 is Sept. 2. Classes begin for kids in grades 1 through 5 with half days on Sept. 2 and 3. Pre-K and Kindergarten begins on Sept. 3 with half days. Stay tuned.
  • Friday, Sept. 11, will mark the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks on the Twin Towers in New York City. It involved four hijacked airliners in coordinated attacks by the Islamic terrorist organization al-Qaeda. Two planes crashed into the Twin Towers, and another was flown into the Pentagon building, which houses the nation’s Department of Defense, in Arlington, Va. There was a passenger mutiny on the fourth jet, which crashed in a field in Shanksville, Pa., instead of its intended target – believed to be the U.S. Capitol or the White House. The Saugus Fire Department is expected to have its normal ceremony late morning on Sept. 11. Meanwhile, Board of Selectmen Chair Debra Panetta and former Selectman Corinne Riley are coordinating a special 9-11 remembrance event at 6 p.m. in front of Saugus Town Hall.
  • On Saturday, Sept. 12, the 45th Annual Saugus Founder’s Day celebration will be held from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. outside Saugus Town Hall and continuing down Central Street and Taylor Street. It’s been called the town’s biggest fund-raising event for nonprofit agencies and various community groups. Founder’s Day will once again offer residents the opportunity to come together to show their Saugus pride while they stroll past more than 100 booths set up for the celebration. There will be food, craft and informational booths set up. There will be various entertainment performances involving music, theatre and dance groups. The highlight of this huge community social occasion will be the presentation of this year’s Saugus Persons of the Year 2026 recipients – a “Man of the Year” and a “Woman of the Year.” A list of the recipients dating back to 1989 will be read as part of the ceremony. A makeshift stage will be set up on the steps of Saugus Town Hall for living “Person of the Year” recipients to sit and welcome the two honorees they voted on for this year’s presentation.
  • On Monday, Sept. 14, there will be a vigil in front of Saugus Town Hall at 6:30 p.m. for Saugus to come together as a community to remember the lives the town has lost due to overdose and suicide.
  • Saugus Olympics Day at World Series Park in Saugus will be held on Saturday, Sept. 26, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Nancy Kerrigan, a former Olympics medalist, will take part in the opening ceremony and will be available to meet and greet those in attendance. Other former Olympics medalists, including athletes who competed in this year’s Winter Olympics, have been invited. Funds raised from the event will go to Challenger Baseball and Boys & Girls Club. A baseball tournament involving Challenger Baseball teams from the area will start at 9 a.m. At 11 a.m. the opening ceremony and parade of athletes will take place.

If I missed any important September events, please email me at mv***@*****st.net. Or feel free to post your announcement on “The Sounds of Saugus” column on our Advocate Newspapers Facebook Page.

 

Early In-Person voting starts tomorrow

For those civic-minded Saugonians who want to get it over with, In-Person Early Voting for the Sept. 1 State Primary Election will begin tomorrow (Saturday, Aug. 22) from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. in the Community Room of the Saugus Public Library at 295 Central St. Voters should enter through the Taylor Street Entrance. This is also the last day to register to vote in the election.

In-Person Early Voting will be held for five additional days next week, as follows:

  • Monday, August 24, 2026 – 8:30 a.m.to 7:00 p.m.
  • Tuesday, August 25, 2026 – 8:15 a.m.to 4:00 p.m.
  • Wednesday, August 26, 2026 – 8:15 a.m.to 4:00 p.m.
  • Thursday, August 27, 2026 – 8:15 a.m.to 4:00 p.m.
  • Friday, August 28, 2026 – 8:15 a.m.to 12:30 p.m.

In addition, every registered voter has the option to vote by mail if they want. All registered voters in the state should have received a “Vote by Mail Application” with a postage-free postcard to mail to a Town or City Clerk’s Office. The deadline to mail back the application to receive a mail-in ballot is 5 p.m. next Tuesday (Aug. 25). To receive a primary ballot, the voter must select Democratic or Republican on the postcard. Voting by mail-in ballot in a primary will not enroll you in a political party. For more information about your voting options for the Sept. 1 State Primary Election, please call 781-231-4101 or 781-231-4102.

 

Saugus United Parish Food Pantry

The Saugus United Parish Food Pantry will be open today (Friday, August 21) from 9:30-11 a.m. at 50 Essex St. in the basement of Cliftondale Congregational Church. The food pantry welcomes all neighbors facing food insecurity on Friday mornings. Volunteers are also welcome. Please call the Food Pantry Office (781-233-2663) or go to the website (cliftondalecc.org) for details.

 

Summer Reading Program ends today

By all accounts, it’s been another fun and successful year for the Saugus Public Library’s Summer Reading Program. And everybody who participated was a winner – because they honed their reading skills while also earning prizes, according to Amy Melton, Head of Children’s Services at the library. The last day to pick up prizes is today (Friday, August 21), she said.

“So keep reading, keep earning prizes, and keep your reading adventure going! We’re grateful to the New Friends of the Saugus Library and the Saugus Library Foundation for their generous support of this year’s program,” Amy said.

 

This week’s “Shout Outs”

At this week’s (Tuesday, Aug. 18) Board of Selectmen’s meeting, the board’s chair, Debra Panetta, offered a special “Shout Out” – for the benefit of Saugus TV viewers as well as Saugus Advocate readers – to the board’s clerk, Meredith Casagrande, for the preparation that went into the seven public hearings that were held: “Meredith worked super hard to get all of these hearings in order and make sure that everything was in proper order and proper format. And I know that she literally jumped through hoops to get everything for us tonight so nothing had to be continued. So, thank you Meredith, for going over and above. We appreciate it.”

Selectman Michael Serino quipped, good naturedly: “Thanks Meredith. Don’t fall when you jump through that hoop.”

Saugus Council on Aging Director Laurie Davis publicly thanked the selectmen in a recent letter for accepting two new vehicles for the Saugus Council on Aging to support the transportation needs of the town’s senior residents: “The first vehicle is a 2026 Ford Transit 11-passenger van, which will be used to transport seniors safely to and from the Saugus Senior Center, as well as provide transportation for grocery shopping and other Council on Aging programs and activities. This vehicle will help us continue to provide reliable, accessible transportation while meeting the growing needs of our senior population.

“The second vehicle is a 2026 Toyota Camry Hybrid, which will be used primarily to transport seniors to and from medical appointments. As you know, access to dependable transportation is essential for many older adults to attend medical visits, receive treatments and maintain their health and independence.”

A special “Shout Out” from The Saugus Advocate editor to Saugonian Millie Doucette, who celebrated her 101st birthday today (Friday, Aug. 21). In an interview last year for “The Advocate Asks,” Millie shared some advice on how to live to be 100. She credited her faith in God, holistic medicine, a great personal doctor, diet and exercise – and a lot of dancing. She is an Everett native, but has spent more than 60 years of her life in a house on Clifton Avenue. All three of her children were students of Saugus Public Schools and graduated from Saugus High.

 

Want to “Shout Out” a fellow Saugonian?

This is an opportunity for our paper’s readers to single out – in a brief mention – remarkable acts or achievements by Saugus residents or an act of kindness or a nice gesture. Just send an email (mv***@*****st.net) with a mention in the subject line of “An Extra Shout Out.” No more than a paragraph; anything longer might lend itself to a story and/or a photo.

 

A makeup free concert for Aug. 26

People who have been going to the free Summer Concert Series will be happy to know that there will be one more next week. Ditto Band, which specializes in Acoustic American Rock, will be performing at the Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site next Wednesday (Aug. 26) from 5:30-7:30 p.m. The group was scheduled to play on July 29, but inclement weather led to the concert’s cancellation. Next week’s concert concludes the eight-week-long Summer Concert Series at the Iron Works, which will begin at 5:30 on the stage behind the museum building.

Spectators can settle down on the upper lawn. People can bring blankets and chairs, snacks, etc. Don’t forget to bring a friend, too, to enjoy a couple of hours of music outdoors.

This marks the fifth consecutive summer that the Saugus Public Library and the National Park Service have collaborated on a local outdoor event that seems to get more popular every year. The Saugus Cultural Council (a local arm of the Mass Cultural Council, a state agency) is also a key sponsor of the event.

The concert series celebrates local musical talents in Essex County and creates opportunities for residents and visitors to engage with the park during evening hours. It is suitable for all ages. Restrooms are available until nearly 8 p.m., when the concert concludes. If the weather looks bad, concertgoers are urged to check the library website (www.sauguspubliclibrary.org), which will update for cancellations on that day.

 

Summer Street paving set to begin on Monday

The Town of Saugus announced that National Grid is scheduled to begin paving operations on Summer Street on Monday (Aug. 24), as final restoration efforts for a major gas main project. Crews will lay down about 2,100 linear feet of pavement on Summer Street, extending from Appleton Street to Main Street, according to a press release issued this week by Town Manager Scott C. Crabtree’s Office. The work will occur on Summer Street and around Appleton Street, Fiske Road, Wilson Street, Summer Court, Pleasant Street, Prospect Street, Parker Street, Taylor Street and Main Street. The work will take place between 7 a.m. and 3 p.m. on Monday (Aug. 24), Tuesday (Aug. 25) and Wednesday (Aug. 26). Police details and detours will be established if necessary.

For questions, please contact Town Engineer Kevin Hallion at 781-231-4032.

 

Saugus Youth Cross Country 2026

With kids headed back to school soon, another season of Saugus Youth Cross Country gets underway. The program, aimed for youth in Grades 1 through 5, will begin its new year on Sept. 1. The Cross Country members run on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 3:45 to 5:15 p.m. at the track behind Belmonte STEAM Academy and on Saturdays from 10:00 to 11:30 a.m. at Breakheart Reservation.

“Cross Country is a sport where athletes run on paths, grass, trails, and parks instead of a track,” said Coach Christopher Tarantino, known popularly as “Coach T,” who oversees the program.

“It is a test of endurance, determination, and heart! Every practice is an adventure and every athlete improves at their own pace,” he said.

“Parents, here’s why your child should get involved! Cross Country is much more than running. It teaches children perseverance, confidence, goal setting, and mental toughness while keeping them active in a fun, encouraging team environment. Through games, age-appropriate training, and positive coaching, children develop lifelong healthy habits, make new friends, build self-confidence, and learn that hard work pays off. Whether your child is already active or just getting started, Cross Country is a welcoming sport where every athlete can succeed,” he said.

The training distances are as follows: from 1st-3rd grades, .7 miles; 4th and 5th, 1.2 miles.

Here are some program highlights:

  • Practice races Saturdays TBD at Frey Park in Lynn Mass., at 285 Walnut St.
  • Varied Saturday practice locations to be determined
  • Saturday, Oct. 31, there will be a Halloween Fun Run practice at Breakheart Reservation.
  • Wednesday, Nov. 11, on Veterans Day, Gannon Golf Course at 60 Great Woods Rd. in Lynn will host the 12th Annual Massachusetts Elementary School Cross Country Championship. Arrival time is set for 8:30 a.m. The race will start at 9:30 a.m. There will be lunch at Prince Pizzeria following the meet. More information TBA.
  • Ending Thursday, November 12: Wrap-up session at Belmonte.

Cost: $150 for first year, $100 returning from Cross Country 2025.

If any questions, further information or to register, please contact Coach T at 781-854-677 or ch********************@***il.com.

 

Veterans Day Bricks Program is Back

The Saugus Veterans Council is pleased to reinstate the Brick Program! After our vendor retired last year (thank you, Del from Pavlok, for working with us over the years), we have found another engraver who will be taking our orders for Veterans Day! Proceeds from the brick sales are devoted to the upkeep of Saugus Veterans Park. If you are interested in purchasing a brick, a 4×8″ is $100 (three lines) and an 8×8″ (five lines) is $200. Please contact Corinne Riley (781-231-7995) for an application or more information. All orders must be in no later than Sept. 10.

news_communities.title: Mystic River Watershed Association and City of Everett unveil new mural at Florence Street Park
news_communities.author: Special to the Record
news_communities.summary:
Officials from the Mystic River Watershed Association (MyRWA) and the City of Everett are pleased to announce the unveiling of a new mural at Florence Street Park (Big Flo). The mural was created by MyRWA’s artist-in-residence, Andres “NXN” Duarte, and features native animal characters playing sports with patterns that represent the local environment. 

“Public art has the ability to transform a space and make it feel more welcoming, vibrant and connected to the community,” said Mayor Robert J. Van Campen. “This mural is a great addition to Florence Street Park because it reflects both how our residents use this space and the natural environment around us. I’m grateful to Andres and the Mystic River Watershed Association for bringing this project to Everett and creating something our community can enjoy for years to come.” 

“I wanted to create something that represents the park and the activities that people do there and connect it to nature and the ecosystems around us,” says Andres “NXN” Duarte. “The animals are all different, just like we are all different, but they are all part of the same community.” 

Andres Duarte is a Boston-based artist born in Bogota, Colombia. He considers himself a tactical urbanist and loves using art to enliven city spaces and change people’s relationship with public space. He has served as the first-ever Mystic River Artist in Residence since 2025. 

The Mystic River Artist in Residence Program is grounded in the belief that creative projects offer unique opportunities to help people connect with and learn about the natural world, making outdoor spaces more accessible and welcoming, and empowering communities to work together to protect and restore the natural resources around us. It is part of the nationwide U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Inaugural Artist-In-Residence Program, which supports a broad range of local artists and culture bearers in six geographic areas within National Estuary Program and Urban Waters Federal Partnership locations, including the Mystic River Watershed Urban Waters Federal Partnership: Massachusetts Bays National Estuary Partnership.

news_communities.title: Encore Harbor Casino in Everett to host Boston Harbor Fight Night 2
news_communities.author: Special to the Record
news_communities.summary:
Undefeated Weymouth middleweight Francis “Frank The Tank” Hogan (22-0, 17 KOs) will headline the “Boston Harbor Fight Night 2” professional boxing card, presented by Granite Chin Promotions and CES Boxing, at Encore Boston Harbor Casino in Everett, Massachusetts. 

The reigning North American Boxing Federation (NABF) Champion, Hogan will throw-down with Ricardo “Bebo” Ruben Villalba (20-12-1, 8 KOs), of Argentina, in the 8-round (non-title fight) main event. 

The 25-year-old Hogan also headlined last November at Encore, also co-promoted by Granite Chin and CES Boxing, in which he thoroughly dominated veteran Antonio Todd for an 8-round unanimous decision.  

Arguably the most promising New England middleweight prospect since Providence’s Demetrius “Boo Boo” Andrade, as well as the best 160-pounder in Massachusetts this century since “Dangerous” Dana Rosenblatt fought as a middleweight, Hogan plans to make a major statement on Aug. 29 that he’s outgrown New England boxing. 

A veteran of 219 amateur matches, Hogan has been boxing since he was 11. The 6’ 2”, southpaw developed into a 2019 New England Golden Gloves Champion, and more on the national level, losing a split decision to Joseph Hicks in the 2019 Olympic Trials. He turned pro in early 2020. 

As an amateur, Hogan sparred with several pros including Marck Deluca, who now trains “Frank The Tank” at Waymaker Boxing gym in Dorchester. Promoted by CES Boxing, he recently signed a managerial contract with Elite Boxing management (Rich Cappiello & Joe Lake). 

Hogan was a devastating puncher when he started training with Deluca, who was a standout amateur and pro boxer (30-4, 18 KOs). 

“I’m more of a boxer-puncher now,” explained Hogan, whose first 10 fights ended in stoppages (only 27 total rounds). “I’m not a brawler anymore, but I’m still exciting to watch! I remember walking out to the ring for my first fight and it sounded crazy. I had never heard a crowd like that and I didn’t want to let people down. People were chanting and stomping their feet. As I started fighting higher level opponents, I realized that I needed to be a ‘clean’ fighter, and I still have a ways to go. 

“Even Canelo (Saul Alvarez) and Triple GGG (Gennady Golovkin) – they knocked out everybody early when the first started — but you can’t keep fighting like that and last. I went back to basics with Mark: jab, hands up, and moving my head. It’s different but that’s what I needed to do to be relaxed in the ring. You have to look in the mirror and work on slipping punches and ring generalship.” 

Hogan’s upcoming opponent, battle-tested Villalba, is a former World Boxing Organization (WBO) and Argentinian Super Middleweight Champion. He’s also become a middleweight gatekeeper, of sorts, having fought leading prospects such as Hicks and Eric Priest.  

“He’s shorter than me, so he’s going to try and fight inside,” Hogan said. “He’s going to get drilled by my jab. I’ll stay relaxed, keep moving my feet as a throw punches, and break him down.” 

A gym rat who is always training when he isn’t working at his job as a licensed welder, Hogan grew into his power punching, but he’s matured in the ring and grown into a legitimate boxer. He can still put opponents to sleep, though, which is routinely known as, “Tank Time!” 

Scituate heavyweight Kevin “Big Gulp” Nagle (11-8, 8 KOs), the former WBC USA Silver and Massachusetts Heavyweight Champion, takes on Misfits Heavyweight title-holder Chase “Mr. Belt To Ass” Demoor (6-2-1, 6 KOs) in an 8-rounder. 

Former Massachusetts Middleweight Champion Anthony “The Gentle Savage” Andreozzi (7-6-1, 3 KOs), fighting out of Swansea, MA, faces New Hampshire rival Ryan Clark (5-8-1, 2 KOs) in a 6-rounder. In 2024, Andreozzi won a 3-round split decision over Clark in a Granite Chin tournament. 

Milton bantamweight Jenn Perella (5-1, 1 KO), former 2024 National Golden Gloves finalist and 2-time New England Golden Gloves Champion, has dropped down one weight class for her 6-round bout versus Chantal Sumrall. 

Dorchester junior welterweight Jonathan de Pina (15-2, 7 KOs), a 2018 New England Golden Gloves Champion, fights Anthony “Toro Rojo” Mora (7-9-1, 4 KOs) in an another 6-rounder. 

Undefeated junior middleweight Jaydell The Pazmanian Devil” Pazmino (9-0, 8 KOs), fighting out Londonderry, New Hampshire, who was a 2020 New England Golden Gloves Champion, risks his perfect pro record against upset-minded Alfred Raymond, of Warwick, Rhode Island, in a 6-rounder. 

Five-time national amateur champion Melanie “The Pitbull” Costa (3-1, 1 KO), a Norton police officer, returns to the ring in a 4-round bantamweight encounter with Brittany Dukes 

Revere light heavyweight Leonardo Ladeira (8-11-1, 7 KOs) will fight Everet DeSilets in a 6-round fight. 

Former college basketball player Barrett Hanlon, of Hopkinton (MA), will make his pro debut against Ratavious Thrasher in a 4-round light heavyweight match. 

Once again, Granite Chin Promotions has partnered with the Quincy Fire Cancer Foundation for “Boston Harbor Fight Night 2” to raise awareness and support for this most worthy charitable organization. For more information go online to www.quincyfirecancerfoundation.com. 

Card subject to change. 

Tickets are available to purchase online at www.GraniteChin.ticketspice.com and www.CESBoxing.com. 

Doors open at 5 p.m. ET, first bout at 7 p.m. ET.

news_communities.title: DiDomenico votes to save ratepayers money on energy costs
news_communities.author: Special to the Record
news_communities.summary:
Senator Sal DiDomenico and his colleagues in the Massachusetts Senate passed energy affordability legislation that is projected to deliver billions in savings to ratepayers across the Commonwealth while keeping Massachusetts on track to meet its climate goals.  

The bill, S.3143, An Act to save people money, repair the climate, and grow the economy, tackles rising energy costs head-on by cutting unnecessary fees, evening out price spikes that hit households during high-demand months, cracking down on predatory sales practices by energy suppliers, and steering the state away from expensive infrastructure projects that don’t deliver value for ratepayers.  

“Energy bills have been too high in recent years and for people across my district, especially those with lower income, this can force impossible decisions on people like paying for the heat or paying for groceries. I am thrilled to move this legislation forward that will bring down energy costs and accelerate our state’s transition to renewable energy with less pollution,” said Senator Sal DiDomenico. “There has been a false narrative that we can either lower ratepayer bills or advance clean energy, when the reality has always been that you need one to do the other. This bill does exactly that, by marrying efficiency programs and clean energy development with customer protections and cutting red tape, we are continuing our state’s climate commitments and ensuring electricity and heat is affordable for everyone.” 

The legislation targets the biggest cost drivers that Massachusetts residents face on their monthly bills, including fees, surcharges, and rate adjustments.  

 

Cutting Out the Intermediary on Energy  

Purchasing — Up to $420 Million in Savings  

Right now, utility companies act as intermediaries when Massachusetts buys clean energy, and they collect a fee for that role. This bill lets the state negotiate those contracts directly, cutting out the fee and saving ratepayers up to $420 million.  

 

Evening Out Seasonal  

Price Spikes —  

$780 Million in Savings  

Energy prices for customers on basic service contracts are currently locked in every six months, which can cause sudden jumps in what residents pay. The bill gives regulators more flexibility in how and when prices are set, which is expected to save ratepayers $780 million.  

 

Reviewing Hidden Charges That Spike During Peak Months —  

$750 Million in Savings  

Bills often include separate ‘reconciling charges’ that aren’t reviewed consistently. The bill requires regulators to reform these charges, particularly ones that spike during high-demand months, which will save residents an estimated $750 million.  

 

Investigating Markups on Electric Bills — Up to  

$1 Billion in Savings  

A new state investigation will examine whether customers have been overcharged when utilities didn’t actively shop for the best electricity rates. Between 2015 and 2024, Massachusetts customers may have paid an estimated $3.4 billion more than necessary. This investigation could lead to savings of up to $1 billion, or roughly $12 a month for a typical household.  

 

Cracking Down on Predatory Energy Suppliers — More Than $650 Million  

in Savings  

So-called ‘competitive’ energy suppliers have used aggressive sales tactics to lure customers in with low introductory rates only to sharply raise prices later. Over the past decade, customers who switched to these suppliers paid an estimated $738.7 million more than if they’d simply stayed with their regular utility. The bill strengthens consumer protections and enforcement, to save ratepayers a projected $650 million.  

 

Helping Utilities Pay Down Debt Without Passing It to Customers — Up to $7.1 Billion in Savings  

The bill allows utility companies to finance certain costs, like those from storm recovery and grid upgrades, at lower interest rates instead of borrowing at higher costs and passing those costs on to residents. This alone could save ratepayers up to $7.1 billion over 10 years.  

 

Streamlining the Gas Pipe Repair Program —  

$1.46 Billion in Savings  

The Gas System Enhancement Plan, a program meant to incentivize utilities to fix aging, leak-prone gas pipes, has ballooned in cost, making up an estimated eight to 11 per cent of a typical gas bill, while allowing companies to skip standard cost reviews. The bill narrows the program to focus only on pipes that actually need repair, phases it out by 2030, and restores normal oversight, saving ratepayers an estimated $1.46 billion.  

 

Making Solar and Clean Energy More Affordable Up Front — $540 Million in Savings  

For homeowners who want to install solar panels or battery storage but can’t afford the upfront cost, the bill creates a way to finance that equipment through their utility bill over time. By doing so, it potentially saves consumers $540 million as more households take advantage of it.  

 

Cutting Red Tape in  

Energy Planning —  

$1.7 Billion in Savings  

Utility companies currently plan infrastructure projects through multiple, disconnected approval processes, which can overwhelm regulators and often lead to duplicated or unnecessary spending. The bill requires a single, streamlined planning process, helping avoid wasteful projects and saving residents an estimated $1.7 billion.  

 

Strengthening the Mass Save Program  

The legislation strengthens the Mass Save program, which helps residents weatherize homes and upgrade to energy-efficient equipment, by making it more accountable and effective. The bill caps the program’s administrative spending, removes a requirement that utility companies automatically receive bonus payments, and creates a new oversight board to keep the program focused on results.  

 

Protecting Massachusetts’ Climate Leadership  

The bill preserves the state’s commitment to clean energy by adjusting the pace of certain renewable energy purchasing requirements to reflect federal setbacks to offshore wind, supporting renewable natural gas made from food and organic waste, and allowing outside investment in upgrading the electric grid to handle growing demand.  

Having passed both chambers of the Legislature, the bill will now go through a reconciliation process to resolve differences before a final version is sent to the Governor.

news_communities.title: New England Patriots invite Chelsea students, CHS football and CPD’s Build the Base team to attend 2026 preseason game
news_communities.author: Special to the Record
news_communities.summary:
The New England Patriots invited 100 Chelsea community members including Chelsea Public Schools students, Chelsea High School football players and members of the Chelsea Police Department’s Build the Base program to attend the Patriots’ preseason opener last Thursday at Gillette Stadium, extending a gracious opportunity for Chelsea youth and community members to see the defending AFC Champions in action. 

The invitation came after 25 Chelsea High School football student-athletes, accompanied by CHS Football Coach David Roque and Chelsea High School School Resource Officer (SRO) Damian Strait, attended Patriots practice on Saturday, August 1. Strait is the founder of the Build the Base program, an initiative focused on creating positive opportunities for youth through strength and conditioning and physical fitness. The opportunity to attend practice arose from Strait’s work with youth in the community.  

“We are incredibly grateful to the New England Patriots for providing this special opportunity for our Chelsea students and community. Experiences like this create memories that our students will carry with them for years to come,” said CPS Superintendent Dr. Almi G. Abeyta. “Thank you to Officer Damian Strait, Coach David Roque and all of our partners for continuing to open doors and create meaningful opportunities for Chelsea’s young people.”  

“The City of Chelsea couldn’t be more proud to partner with our Public Schools, Police Department, and New England Patriots to give our students this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” said Chelsea City Manager Fidel Maltez. “Chelsea youth need opportunities, especially ones that take them beyond Chelsea, and for that, we are grateful to the Patriots for continuing to do just that.” 

“The Chelsea Police Department is incredibly proud of our ‘Build the Base’ program and the strong partnership we share with the Chelsea Public Schools. Providing our students and the CHS football team with the opportunity to attend the Patriots game is a wonderful testament to this collaboration. Our officers are dedicated to supporting and mentoring these young people, and we are thrilled to see them recognized with such an exciting experience,” Chelsea Police Department Chief Keith E. Houghton added. 

Strait, with support from the Chelsea Police Department, Chelsea Public Schools and community partners, organized two Build the Base Youth Camps for students during February and April school vacation weeks focused on strength, conditioning and discipline for high school students. The work has continued this summer as Strait and Build the Base have worked with Roque on strength and conditioning programs to prepare the Red Devils for the upcoming football season.  

Training Camp for the football team began in August. Chelsea’s first game of the 2026 season is on September 11 at Lowell Catholic at 7:00 p.m. The team’s home opener is on September 25 at 6:00 p.m against Hamilton-Wenham at CHS.

news_communities.title: Chelsea Cultural Council announces 2027 funding applications open September 1
news_communities.author: Special to the Record
news_communities.summary:
The Chelsea Cultural Council (CCC) has announced applications for funding through its 2027 Local Cultural Council (LCC) Grant Program will open at 10 a.m. on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, via the Massachusetts Cultural Council’s SimpleServ application portal available at www.massculturalcouncil.org/communities/local-cultural-council-program/ 

The CCC encourages organizations and individuals planning cultural, educational, and artistic activities that enrich the lives of Chelsea residents in 2027 to apply. The deadline to submit an application is 11:59 p.m. on October 15. 

To support new applications as well as returning applicants, the CCC will host two information sessions: a virtual session on Tuesday, September 8, at 6 p.m., via Zoom, with the Zoom link for the session available at www.chelseama.gov/ccc; and an in-person session on Tuesday, September 22, at 6 p.m. in the Chelsea Public Library basement auditorium at 569 Broadway. 

Every year, the LCC Grant Program funds a variety of Chelsea projects ranging from community events to educational programs that celebrate the city’s diverse cultural heritage. 

In 2026, the program provided nearly $40,000 in grants to support a wide range of community activities such as astronomy nights; the upcoming Mary O’Malley Kite Festival set to take place Saturday, September 25, from 12 to 3 PM; the upcoming Chelsea’s annual Día de los Muertos/Day of the Dead Ofrenda/Altar open to the public from Saturday, October 31, through Sunday, November 1; and several others. 

The Chelsea Cultural Council (CCC) is a volunteer board supported by the Massachusetts Cultural Council. Council members encourage culture and diversity in the City of Chelsea by funding projects in the arts, humanities, and sciences including exhibits, lectures, concerts, festivals, performances, classes, and school field trips. The CCC places an emphasis on locally-based artists and programs that have the greatest impact on the Chelsea community. 

Members of the Council are volunteers appointed by the City Manager for up to two consecutive three-year terms. They consist of artists, arts administrators, and other community members interested in local public arts and cultural programming.  

For more information visit www.chelseama.gov/ccc, and with questions, please contact culturalcouncil@chelseama.gov.

news_communities.title: West Nile Virus confirmed in mosquito from Chelsea
news_communities.author: Special to the Record
news_communities.summary:
The Massachusetts Department of Public Health (MDPH) announced that West Nile virus (WNV) has been detected in a mosquito collected from Chelsea, Massachusetts. 

WNV is most commonly transmitted to humans by the bite of an infected mosquito. The mosquitoes that carry this virus are common throughout the state and are found in urban as well as more rural areas. While WNV can infect people of all ages, people over the age of 50 are at higher risk for severe infection.  

By taking a few, common sense precautions, people can help to protect themselves and their loved ones: 

Avoid Mosquito Bites 

• Apply Insect Repellent when you go outdoors. Use a repellent with DEET (N, N-diethyl-m-toluamide), permethrin, picaridin (KBR 3023), IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus [p-methane 3, 8-diol (PMD)] according to the instructions on the product label. DEET products should not be used on infants under two months of age and should be used in concentrations of 30% or less on older children. Oil of lemon eucalyptus should not be used on children under three years of age. Permethrin products are intended for use on items such as clothing, shoes, bed nets and camping gear and should not be applied to skin.  

• Clothing Can Help reduce mosquito bites. Although it may be difficult to do when it’s hot, wearing long-sleeves, long pants and socks when outdoors will help keep mosquitoes away from your skin. 

• Be Aware of Peak Mosquito Hours – The hours from dusk to dawn are peak biting times for many mosquitoes. When risk is increased, consider rescheduling outdoor activities that occur during evening or early morning. If you are outdoors at any time and notice mosquitoes around you, take steps to avoid being bitten by moving indoors, covering up and/or wearing repellant. 

Mosquito-Proof Your Home 

• Drain Standing Water – Many mosquitoes lay their eggs in standing water. Limit the number of places around your home for mosquitoes to breed by either draining or getting rid of items that hold water. Check rain gutters and drains. Empty any unused flowerpots and wading pools and change water in birdbaths frequently.  

• Install or Repair Screens – Some mosquitoes like to come indoors. Keep them outside by having tightly-fitting screens on all your windows and doors. 

The City of Chelsea will work closely with the MDPH and other agencies, and continue to take preventative measures such as larviciding catch basins throughout the city, a proactive method used to control populations and reduce the spread of diseases like malaria, dengue, and West Nile virus. Larviciding is the practice of applying targeted biological or chemical agents to kill mosquito or blackfly larvae before they mature into flying, biting adults. 

Information about WNV and reports of current and historical WNV virus activity in Massachusetts can be found on the MDPH website at: www.mass.gov/dph/mosquito.  

Tick Bite Prevention Tips 

The City of Chelsea also wishes to provide the community with tick bite prevention tips. Ticks are tiny bugs most likely found in shady, damp, brushy, wooded, or grassy areas (especially in tall grass), including backyards. Ticks do not fly or jump. They attach to animals or people that come into direct contact with them. 

Black-legged (deer) ticks, called deer ticks, can bite you and spread diseases like Lyme disease. The tick usually must be attached to a person for at least 24 hours before it can spread the germ. Black-legged ticks in Massachusetts can also carry the germs that cause babesiosis, human granulocytic anaplasmosis, Powassan virus disease, and Borrelia miyamotoi infection. These ticks are capable of spreading more than one type of germ in a single bite.  

Prevention tips 

One of the most important things you can do is check yourself for ticks once a day. Favorite places ticks like to go on your body include areas between the toes, back of the knees, groin, armpits, and neck, along the hairline, and behind the ears. Remember to check your children and pets, too. Remove any attached ticks as soon as possible. 

• Check yourself, your children and your pets for ticks after coming inside: 

• Inside and behind the ears 

• Along your hairline 

• Back of your neck 

• Armpits 

• Groin 

• Legs 

• Behind your knees 

• Between your toes 

• Ticks are tiny, so look for new “freckles” 

• If you find a tick attached to your skin, don’t panic.  

• Use a pair of fine point tweezers to grip the tick as close to the skin as possible and pull straight out with steady pressure. 

• When going outside to an area likely to have ticks: 

• Stick to main pathways and the center of trails when hiking. 

• Wear a light-colored, long-sleeved shirt with long pants and tuck your pants into your socks. This may be difficult to do when the weather is hot, but it will help keep ticks away from your skin and make it easier to spot a tick on your clothing. 

• Use bug repellents.  

• Repellents that contain DEET can be used on your exposed skin. Permethrin is a product that can be used on your clothes. Always follow the product instructions and use repellents with no more than 30-35% DEET on adults and 10-15% DEET on children. Never use insect repellents on infants.  

More information can be found on MDPH website: www.mass.gov/info-details/tick-borne-disease-prevention.

news_communities.title: News Briefs 8/20/26
news_communities.author: Record Staff
news_communities.summary:
3rd annual 5K Chelsea Road Race set for September 5 

The 3rd Annual Chelsea 5K Road Race is set for Saturday, September 5, at 9:00 AM. New this year is a wheelchair division for both female and male participants. 

The course will follow the same route as in previous years, starting at the rear of the Williams School on Arlington St., turning right onto Sixth St., proceeding up to Washington Ave., and then into Bellingham Sq., from where the runners will proceed down Broadway, framed by the iconic Tobin Bridge. The course turns right onto Second Street and then makes a left to head to Admiral’s Hill, eventually passing under the Tobin to lower Broadway, from where runners will retrace their route back to the Williams School. 

The first 500 registered participants will receive an official race T-shirt as part of their race-day experience. All finishers will be awarded a commemorative medal. 

The entry fee is $25,00, with the fee for the first six wheelchair registrations waived using promo code: CHELSEAUNITED2026. On-line registration is available on raceroster.com. 

Runners can pick up their race bibs on race day in the Williams School playground starting at 7:45. Bibs also can be picked up ahead of time at the Arlington Street entrance of the William school during the following schedule: Wednesday, September 2, 5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.; Thursday, September 3, 4:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.; and Friday, September 4, 4:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m. 

The Chelsea Road Race is organized and managed by the City of Chelsea Department of Recreation & Cultural Affairs. This program is funded in part by the Chelsea Community Fund and a grant from the Chelsea Cultural Council, a local agency which is supported by Mass Cultural Council, a state agency. 

The race has been a huge success for the past two years, drawing a large number of competitors and spectators, and once again is expected to be a festive event for participants of all ages and abilities. 

Chelsea Fire Department Announces 2026 Municipal Firefighter Exam 

Chelsea Fire Chief John Quatieri is encouraging residents interested in a career with the Chelsea Fire Department to take the upcoming 2026 Municipal Firefighter Exam. 

The exam will be held on October 2, 2026, and the deadline to submit an application is August 31, 2026. Interested candidates are encouraged to carefully review the official examination announcement for complete eligibility requirements, application instructions, and other important information. 

“Becoming a firefighter is a great way to serve your community,” said Fire Chief John Quatieri. “The Chelsea Fire Department is looking for individuals who are committed to making a difference.” 

A career with the Fire Department offers the opportunity to serve a diverse community while working alongside dedicated firefighters and officers in a challenging and rewarding profession. 

For additional information and official examination requirements, please visit the City of Chelsea website or the Massachusetts Civil Service website www.mass.gov/info-details/2026-municipal-firefighter-examination. 

Chelsea Residents, Meet Your New Energy Advocate: Adriano Bracero Jimenez  

The Department of Housing & Community Development is pleased to announce Adriano Bracero Jimenez has been named the City’s new Energy Advocate, a role dedicated to connecting residents to energy-related resources and community organizations. Bracero Jimenez, who is trilingual—fluent in English, Spanish, and Portuguese—and has previously worked with the Chelsea residents, is eager to begin working directly with Chelsea’s community members in his new role. 

“As Energy Advocate, I’m excited to provide residents with the information, guidance, and connections they need to make informed decisions based on their unique energy needs and goals,” said Bracero Jimenez. “The Chelsea community can rely on me as a trusted resource and advocate.” 

Bracero Jimenez can help residents who are looking to lower their utility bills, make their home more energy efficient, learn about rebates, and connect with organizations that can help accomplish these tasks. 

Bracero Jimenez previously worked as a community outreach ambassador for the non-profit organization All In Energy where he helped income-eligible residents one-on-one by helping them access discounted utility rates. 

To work with Bracero Jimenez, please contact him directly at abracero@chelseama.gov or call 617-466-4185.

news_communities.title: Man posed as ex-roommate to vote illegally, then reported him, feds say
news_communities.author: Asher Klein
news_communities.summary:
A Chinese man living in Massachusetts impersonated his former roommate, also a Chinese national, to illegally vote on his behalf, then anonymously reported the former roommate to immigration authorities, federal prosecutors said Wednesday.

The apparent revenge scheme — the former roommates ended up with dueling claims in court, according to a criminal complaint — nearly got the former roommate and his wife deported, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Massachusetts.

Yupeng Sun, 33, was arrested on Wednesday on charges of fraudulent voter registration and fraudulent voting, prosecutors said. He was due in federal court in Boston; it wasn’t immediately clear if he had an attorney who could speak to the charge.

According to the criminal complaint, Sun allegedly admitted to investigators last month that he “used his name to vote,” referring to the former roommate, whom he’d confirmed he still had “very, very” bad feelings towards. Sun later texted law enforcement to say he understood it was likely he’d be charged but that he’d been wrongfully arrested and charged because of the man.

The complaint says that Sun rented a room with a Chinese family in Malden from 2021 until May 2023, when Sun was arrested on an assault and battery charge involving the adult daughter of the man he’d later allegedly impersonate. The charges were dismissed over a year later, but Sun claimed in court he’d been unlawfully evicted.

The next year, the man and his wife had forms submitted in their names seeking to give up legal permanent resident status — their green cards. And when they flew back to the U.S. from a trip abroad, they were taken into custody at Logan airport and had the deportation process begun, according to the complaint.

That October, ahead of the presidential election, the man — he wasn’t named in the criminal complaint to protect his and his family’s privacy — had a voter registration application submitted, and an early voting ballot was cast in his name.

Over a year later, the federal agency Homeland Security Investigations began getting tips both online and by mail about the Malden man voting as a non-citizen.

In the meantime, the man and his wife had successfully petitioned the Boston Immigration Court to restore their green cards — they’d testified about their former roommate having access to personal information because he’d helped them apply for insurance, according to the complaint. And when investigators asked him about illegally voting, he said it was possibly Sun who did it to retaliate for his arrest.

If he’s convicted, Sun faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, prosecutors said.

news_communities.title: NeighborHealth promotes safe summer riding through its Annual Children’s Bike Safety Day
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
Families gathered at the East Boston Farmers Market during National Farmer’s Market Week for an afternoon of bike safety education, helmet fittings and community fun

BOSTON, MA (August 7, 2026) – NeighborHealth hosted its annual Children’s Bike Safety Day at the East Boston Farmers Market earlier this week, bringing together local families for an afternoon focused on bike safety, healthy outdoor activity and community connection. With support from Boston Children’s Hospital, the event provided free bike helmets, professional helmet fittings and bike safety education to help children ride safely throughout the summer and beyond.

Designed to promote safe cycling habits and active lifestyles, the event gave families the opportunity to learn about proper helmet use and other important safety practices, all during a special celebration of National Farmers Market Week, offering special activities that highlight the important role local farmer’s play in expanding access to fresh food. Both the bike safety event and Farmer’s Market Week celebration reflect NeighborHealth’s commitment to supporting the health and well-being of children both inside and outside the clinical setting.

The highlight of the event was a bike raffle that awarded six children brand-new bicycles, donated by Boston Children’s Hospital, Excel Academy and First Priority Credit Union. Families were also invited to visit the bike safety tent, where staff from Boston Children’s Hospital provided helmet fittings and shared information about safe riding practices.

“This is truly one of my favorite events of the year,” said Julio Mazul, MD, Executive Vice President and Chief Medical Officer. “There’s nothing quite like seeing a child’s face light up when they hear their name called and realize they’ve just won a new bike. We want every child to experience the fun and freedom that comes with riding a bike, and we’re proud to partner with Boston Children’s Hospital to help ensure families have the equipment and knowledge they need to ride safely all summer long.”

Through its injury prevention efforts, Boston Children’s Hospital provides families with practical safety resources that help reduce the risk of preventable injuries.

“Parents have a lot on their plates, so when we can bring these resources directly into the community, we make it that much easier for families to access them,” said Barbara DiGirolamo, M.Ed., CPSTI, Injury Prevention Program Coordinator at Boston Children’s Hospital. “Whether it’s helping a child find the right helmet fit or answering a parent’s questions about safe riding, these conversations can have a lasting impact.”

Children’s Bike Safety Day was held as part of NeighborHealth’s East Boston Farmers Market, which brings together fresh food vendors, community organizations, health resources and family-focused programming throughout the season. The annual event highlights the power of community partnerships in creating opportunities for children and families to stay healthy, active and connected.

NeighborHealth’s East Boston Farmers Market is held Wednesdays from 3:00 to 6:30 pm, July 8th through October 28th (October hours 3:00–6:00 pm) at Central Square Park in East Boston. This vibrant market, led by Market Manager Kelsey Briggs, attracts hundreds of families weekly and hosts a diverse array of produce and prepared food vendors alongside numerous community essential services and children’s programing.

The market accommodates cash, debit, credit cards, and app payments, and also accepts WIC coupons, Senior coupons, SNAP/food stamps/EBT, P-EBT, and City of Boston Farmers Market coupons, which are available to eligible Boston residents in need of food assistance at the Community Resource Center at 282 Meridian St, East Boston.

For more information about NeighborHealth’s East Boston Farmers Market visit: www.neighborhealth.com.

news_communities.title: Two hundred fifty kids Boston kids had a blast at Save the Harbor’s Annual Eastie Beach Bash
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
AUGUST 18, 2025, BOSTON – On August 11, 2025, 250 children beat the heat at Save the Harbor/Save the Bay’s annual East Boston Beach Bash on Constitution Beach in East Boston.

Children from all over Boston had a memorable time playing cornhole with the New England Revolution, cooling off with slushies from ZnZ slushies, and practicing their juggling and hula hooping with the Boston Circus Guild. 

They also swam and kayaked with the Neighborhood of Affordable Housing in the clean East Boston waters. According to Save the Harbor’s 2025 Water Quality Report Card, Constitution Beach scored a high 93% water quality rating. 

Not only did the kids have fun, but they also learned about the Boston’s marine environment through activities facilitated by Massachusetts Water Resources Authority and Stone Living Lab. Save the Harbor youth staff also facilitated an interactive touch tank containing green crabs and mussels.

“The East Boston Beach Bash gives kids the opportunity to connect with Boston Harbor at a young age,” said Save The Harbor Executive Director Chris Mancini. “We hope that they form fond memories of Boston and its beaches that eventually inspire them to be the next generation of environmental stewards. They might even apply to be part of our youth staff once they reach high school!”

“The East Boston community is grateful to have such an amazing and impactful event that lets our youth deepen their relationship to our local public beach,” said Representative Adrian Madaro, Co-Chair of the Metropolitan Beaches Commission. “Every summer, we look forward to activating our beach in a fun and engaging way for the public to enjoy.”

This event was made possible through funding coming from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts and from Save the Harbor’s annual Shamrock Splash fundraiser. Save the Harbor is especially grateful for the support of the Healey-Driscoll administration, Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs, JetBlue, the Coca-Cola Company, Massport, Liberty Mutual Foundation, Blue Cross Blue Shield of MA, Bay State Cruise Company, Mass Bay Lines, and Eastern Salt.

About Save the Harbor/Save the Bay

Save the Harbor/Save the Bay is the region’s leading voice for clean water and continued public investment in Boston Harbor, the region’s public beaches, and the Boston Harbor Islands. Since 1986, our mission has been to restore and protect Boston Harbor, Massachusetts Bay, and the marine environment, and share them with the public for everyone to enjoy. 

Save the Harbor is committed to making Boston Harbor, the Islands, our beaches, and our programs inclusive, equitable, diverse, and accessible to everyone and anyone. We provide free programs, events and create opportunities for people to experience Boston Harbor and our spectacular urban natural resources first-hand, with an emphasis on breaking down barriers of race, language, income and ability.

Photos by Katy Rogers Art.

news_communities.title: A beautiful day: Number 37 of Eastie Pride Day was grand
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
(EAST BOSTON, August 15, 2026) Piers Park was filled with fun and entertainment as hundreds gathered to express their pride in East Boston. Organizers rolled out the 37th edition of the event on a picture perfect day along the East Boston waterfront.

The family-friendly celebration is always open to all, aiming to bring the community of East Boston together to connect with restaurants, local small businesses, and non-profit organizations. On hand was a variety of food and refreshments, live entertainment, games for children, music, and several contests.

The current Chair of the Committee, Liana LaMattina, says, “We are excited to have created a space for members of our community to celebrate East Boston, connect with one another, and to continue the tradition of Eastie Pride Day for another year.”

More photographs by EastBoston.com available here.

The mission of the event is to encourag pride in East Boston since it was hosted for the first time by Sal LaMattina in 1989. Eastie Pride Day has continued to be an event that community members of all ages look forward to each summer, and the Committee is very grateful to the sponsors who make this celebration possible and can help it continue to grow. It is one of the events that make East Boston, a diverse welcoming community unique in the city. Eastie Pride Day is made possible through the hard work of a neighborhood committee that serves the East Boston community through an annual summer community celebration. This event is meant to highlight the values and qualities of the neighborhood, while also fostering a sense of unity and pride for residents.

news_communities.title: Learning how food brings us together
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
BY MARCIE ASARO

During the last five weeks, my first-grade students at the EB Early Education Center in the Summer Early Focus program have been studying how food brings us together. Our guiding question for the unit was: “How does the food system we are building help create community?”

Throughout this time, the students learned about food justice and affordable, nutritious food access for all. To see this in action, our class took a community walk to three local businesses: Carmella’s, A & L Bakery, and Eastie Farms.

The children were met with such kind and friendly faces at every stop and asked wonderful questions:

Carmella’s: When the students asked owner Nick, “How do you support our community here in East Boston?” he replied, “I give back to school functions and donate pizza and other types of sandwiches to schools. If your school was having a special occasion, I would be more than happy to donate to help my community of young learners.”

A & L Bakery: When asked by the students, “Do you help support our community?” owner Rita answered, “Yes, I give to the East Boston oup Kitchen and special holiday events around Christmas and Easter time.”

Eastie Farms (on Summer Street): Two young gentlemen were hard at work keeping up with the garden when we stopped by. They invited us in, let the students explore, and described what they were growing. The students asked if anything was ready to be harvested; four carrots were ready, so four lucky students were able to pick them! When the children asked, “How does Eastie Farms help families in East Boston?” one of the farmers explained, “Eastie Farms has many programs. We partner with schools around our community, and we also have programs where we show families how to start a garden in their own space. Since East Boston doesn’t have much land, we show people how to use the space they have to grow their own nutritious fruit and veggies so they have access to healthy foods.”

I would like to sincerely thank these three local businesses for opening their doors and gates to my students, donating special treats, and simply being there for our community when we need them.

Throughout this process, the students even built their own model food systems using boxes to demonstrate how they would help their community. We had so many wonderful student-generated ideas, including:

 An elder care convenience store, a bakery, and a free-bites restaurant.

 An Asian restaurant and an Asian convenience store with affordable prices for all.

 A shelter and food pantry providing a safe night’s sleep and food to eat.

 An ice cream store that children can easily access.

 A donation bank where people can drop off nutritious food for others to take.

 A fancy restaurant featuring a donation-based payment model.

I am super proud of the students and how much they have learned over these five weeks. A huge shout-out to our community for opening your doors, donating treats, answering questions, and showing our young learners how to give back to East Boston and find resources if needed!

news_communities.title: NeighborHealth appoints Dr. Pablo Buitron de la Vega as Vice President and Associate Chief Medical Officer
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
BOSTON, MA (August 14, 2026) – NeighborHealth today announced the appointment of Pablo Buitron de la Vega, MD, MSc, as Vice President and Associate Chief Medical Officer of the state’s largest community health center. A preventive medicine physician leader, Dr. Buitron de la Vega will help advance NeighborHealth’s clinical quality, population health and health equity goals across the communities it serves.

Dr. Buitron de la Vega joins NeighborHealth from Boston Medical Center (BMC), where he served as an internal medicine primary care physician and built programs that made screening and referral for social needs, such as food, housing and transportation, a routine part of clinical care. He is known for designing practical workflows and technology that allow care teams to scale solutions across busy clinical settings.

“Dr. Buitron de la Vega brings tremendous clinical expertise and a deep understanding of the factors that shape the health of our patients and communities,” said Julio Mazul, MD, Executive Vice President and Chief Medical Officer at NeighborHealth. “We know that what happens outside of the exam room can be just as important as what happens inside. Pablo’s leadership will strengthen our ability to reduce barriers to care, improve outcomes and deliver high-quality, culturally responsive care to every patient.”

In his new role, Dr. Buitron de la Vega will work alongside Dr. Mazul and NeighborHealth’s leadership team to advance clinical quality and innovative care models that address persistent health disparities. His appointment builds on NeighborHealth’s longstanding commitment to challenging the systemic barriers that have disproportionately affected low-income, immigrant and historically marginalized communities.

“NeighborHealth’s mission deeply resonates with why I became a physician and why I have devoted my career to addressing social drivers of health,” said Dr. Buitron de la Vega, who grew up in Quito, Ecuador, trained there as a physician and now lives in Roxbury. “Improving health means understanding the full context of our patients’ lives — and then doing the harder work of designing systems that respond to those needs with dignity and respect. Much of my career has been spent finding practical ways to innovate in real-world community settings. I am excited to join NeighborHealth and help translate our commitment to health equity into better outcomes for the communities we serve.”

Dr. Buitron de la Vega’s appointment further strengthens the clinical leadership team led by Dr. Mazul, who was named Chief Medical Officer in 2025 after nearly two decades at NeighborHealth. Dr. Mazul has led efforts to advance patient safety and clinical quality while expanding culturally responsive care for NeighborHealth’s diverse patient population.

Dr. Buitron de la Vega earned his medical degree from Pontificia Universidad Católica del Ecuador and completed his internal medicine residency at Henry Ford Hospital in Detroit, Michigan. He later completed training in preventive medicine and earned a Master of Science from Boston University School of Public Health. At BMC, he served as a primary care physician and as Program Director of the Preventive Medicine Residency Program, where he founded a fellowship track in immigrant and refugee health. He also led BMC’s THRIVE program, which he helped grow from a single-department initiative into an institution-wide, Joint Commission–recognized model that reaches more than 100,000 patients annually.

Alongside his role at NeighborHealth, he holds a faculty appointment as an Assistant Professor of Medicine at Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine and advises BMC’s THRIVE program.

About NeighborHealth

NeighborHealth, formerly East Boston Neighborhood Health Center, is one of the nation’s largest Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) and the largest community-based primary care health system in Massachusetts, serving over 120,000 people and recognized by the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) as a National Quality Leader. For more than 55 years, NeighborHealth has offered access to comprehensive primary care, specialty care and emergency care for patients in the Commonwealth. In a first-of-its-kind merger in 2020, East Boston Neighborhood Health Center joined forces with the South End Community Health Center and expanded services to patients who live and work in Boston’s South End and Roxbury neighborhoods. NeighborHealth champions innovative care models to actively bridge health equity gaps in our low-income and immigrant communities with services unique from other healthcare providers in our state. For more information, visit www.neighborhealth.com.
